rows.branch: All branches (the Four Books are held by the Cheng-Zhu and Lu-Wang schools and by modern New Confucians alike)
rows.reference: Mencius 7A.33 (ctext Jin Xin I, 33; Legge VII.A.33; Kanripo inline 13.33)
rows.original: 殺一無罪、非仁也，非其有而取之、非義也
rows.translation: Chinese read in Kanripo KR1h0001 (TLS base text); Legge (1861; 1895) not displayed; paraphrase is the project's own
rows.says: Prince Dian asks what a scholar's business is. Mencius says: to set his aims high (尚志), which means humaneness and rightness and nothing more. To kill one person who has done no wrong is against humaneness; to take what is not yours is against rightness.
rows.bearing: K1: Explicit for every innocent person. It sets no limit by status, sex, age or faith, so by its plain words it reaches newborns, wives, servants, slaves and strangers (rules 7 and 9). It does not say who may kill the guilty; Mencius 2B.8 does. K0: Explicit for every innocent victim, whatever the motive. Now verified, so it decides (rule 1).

rows.reference: Mencius 2A.2 (ctext Gong Sun Chou I, 2; Legge II.A.2; Kanripo inline 3.2), near the end of the chapter
rows.original: 行一不義，殺一不辜，而得天下，皆不為也
rows.translation: Chinese read in Kanripo KR1h0001 (TLS base text); Legge (1861; 1895) not displayed; paraphrase is the project's own
rows.says: Asked whether Bo Yi, Yi Yin and Confucius had anything in common, Mencius says yes: given a hundred li of land to rule, each could have brought the lords to his court and held the realm, but none of them would have done one unrighteous act or killed one innocent person to gain the realm.
rows.bearing: K1: Explicit that the tradition's model sages would not kill one innocent person even for the greatest possible gain; it reaches every innocent person (rule 7). K0 (gain): Explicit. Now verified, so it decides (rule 1).

rows.reference: Mencius 2B.8 (ctext Gong Sun Chou II, 8; Legge II.B.8; Kanripo inline 4.8)
rows.original: 彼如曰：『孰可以殺之？』則將應之曰：『為士師，則可以殺之。』
rows.translation: Chinese read in Kanripo KR1h0001 (TLS base text); Legge (1861; 1895) not displayed; paraphrase is the project's own
rows.says: Shen Tong asks privately whether Yan may be attacked, and Mencius says it may. When Qi attacks Yan, someone asks whether Mencius urged it. He says no: had he been asked who may attack it, he would have said only a 'minister of Heaven' (天吏). In the same way, if asked whether a man who has killed someone may be put to death, he would say yes; if asked who may do it, he would say the criminal judge (士師). Qi attacking Yan is 'Yan attacking Yan' (以燕伐燕), so why would he have urged it?
rows.bearing: K1 and K0: Clear teaching that even a killer may be put to death only by the officer of justice, never by someone acting on his own authority. It reaches the guilty, whom 7A.33 does not cover, and it is the counted answer to the revenge duty in the uncounted Book of Rites (rule 5 reach of K1; revenge clause of K0). The judge's killing is court context and the attack on Yan is war (rule 5). Clear teaching, not Explicit, because it is an analogy inside an argument about war, though its premise is stated as plainly true. Now verified, so it decides (rule 1).

rows.reference: Mencius 7B.31 (ctext Jin Xin II, 31; Legge VII.B.31; Kanripo inline 14.31)
rows.original: 人能充無欲害人之心，而仁不可勝用也
rows.translation: Chinese read in Kanripo KR1h0001 (TLS base text); Legge (1861; 1895) not displayed; paraphrase is the project's own
rows.says: Everyone has things they cannot bear to do; extending this to what they can bear is humaneness. Everyone has things they will not do; extending this to what they will do is rightness. If a person fills out the heart that does not wish to harm others, their humaneness will be more than they can use.
rows.bearing: K1 and K0: a wider rule (rule 7). The heart that does not wish to harm anyone is the root of humaneness, owed to everyone. Clear teaching, not Explicit, because it is framed as self-cultivation. Now verified with its number; it supports the labels but is not needed, since 7A.33, 2A.2 and 2B.8 decide.

rows.reference: Analects 15.24 (ctext Wei Ling Gong 24; Legge XV.23) and 12.2 (ctext Yan Yuan 2; Legge XII.2)
rows.original: 其恕乎！己所不欲，勿施於人
rows.translation: James Legge (1861; 1893), as recorded in Article I; Chinese read in Kanripo KR1h0004
rows.says: What you do not want for yourself, do not impose on others. Confucius gives it to Zigong as the one word to practise all one's life, naming it 恕 (15.24), and to Zhonggong as part of his answer on humaneness, followed by 'no resentment in the state, none in the family' (12.2).
rows.bearing: K1 and K0: a wider rule (rule 7). No one wants to be killed, so the rule forbids killing others, and it reaches every person; Zhu Xi glosses it as extending oneself to others and things generally (推己及物, verified by search in Article I research). The households annex accepted these rows for L1 by the same route (CO-2). They now support the labels rather than carry them alone, since Mencius 7A.33, 2A.2 and 2B.8 are verified. Limits: the rule is a test of conduct, not a rule about killing; it names no exception for defence (K1 does not need one); and the uncounted classics show that the historical tradition held it together with a duty of revenge.
rows.strength: Clear teaching (wider rule; the rule itself is Explicit)

rows.branch: All branches (the Lu-Wang school reads the Great Learning in the older Book of Rites order, but the passage is in both)
rows.reference: Great Learning, commentary ch. 10 (Zhu Xi's arrangement)
rows.original: 所惡於上，毋以使下 … 此之謂絜矩之道
rows.translation: James Legge (1861)
rows.says: What you dislike from those above you, do not do to those below you, and so in every direction: this is the way of the measuring square.
rows.bearing: K1 and K0: a wider rule (rule 7) addressed to anyone with power over others, so it reaches the masters, parents and husbands K1 binds. Same limits as Analects 15.24. Counted as primary, but the labels do not depend on it, because the Tier 1 Mencius and Analects rows decide.

rows.original: 忠恕違道不遠，施諸己而不願，亦勿施於人
rows.translation: James Legge (1861), as on ctext; paraphrased
rows.says: Loyalty and consideration are not far from the Way: what you would not wish done to yourself, do not do to others.
rows.bearing: K1 and K0: the same wider rule (rule 7) in a text treated as primary. Supporting only; not needed for any label.

rows.reference: Analects 12.22 (ctext Yan Yuan 22; Legge XII.22); Mencius 4B.28 (ctext Li Lou II, 28; Legge IV.B.28; Kanripo inline 8.28), first half
rows.original: 樊遲問仁。子曰：「愛人。」 ; 仁者愛人，有禮者敬人
rows.translation: Chinese read in Kanripo KR1h0004 and KR1h0001; Legge not displayed; paraphrase is the project's own
rows.says: Asked what humaneness is, Confucius says: love people. Mencius says the humane person loves others and the person of propriety respects others; whoever loves others is loved by them.
rows.bearing: Implied for K1: it states an attitude, not a rule of conduct, and the same texts accept a ruler's punishments. Not needed for any label.

rows.reference: Mencius 4B.28 (ctext Li Lou II, 28; Legge IV.B.28; Kanripo inline 8.28), second half
rows.original: 其待我以橫逆，則君子必自反也 … 此亦妄人也已矣。如此，則與禽獸奚擇哉？於禽獸又何難焉？
rows.translation: Chinese read in Kanripo KR1h0001 (TLS base text); Legge (1861; 1895) not displayed; paraphrase is the project's own
rows.says: If someone treats the noble person with outrage, he turns back on himself: he must have lacked humaneness or propriety; then he asks whether he lacked loyalty. If the outrage still continues, he says: this is simply a reckless man, no different from a beast, and why should I trouble myself over a beast? The noble person has a lifelong concern (to become like Shun) but no single morning's trouble.
rows.bearing: K0 (revenge for wrongs to oneself): Clear teaching that outrage is answered by self-examination, not by contending with the offender; a wider rule against retaliation (rule 7), but it does not name killing and does not reach wrongs done to one's kin. Calling the offender a beast is not a licence to harm him: the point is that he is not worth contending with. Now verified; it supports K0 but is not needed to decide it.
rows.strength: Clear teaching (wider rule, wrongs to oneself)

rows.reference: Mencius 2A.6 (ctext Gong Sun Chou I, 6; Legge II.A.6; Kanripo inline 3.6) and 3A.5 (ctext Teng Wen Gong I, 5; Legge III.A.5; Kanripo inline 5.5)
rows.original: 乍見孺子將入於井，皆有怵惕惻隱之心 ; 赤子匍匐將入井，非赤子之罪也
rows.translation: Chinese read in Kanripo KR1h0001 (TLS base text); Legge (1861; 1895) not displayed; paraphrase is the project's own
rows.says: 2A.6: everyone has a heart that cannot bear others' suffering; anyone who suddenly sees a small child about to fall into a well feels alarm and pity, not to win the parents' favour or the neighbours' praise; whoever lacks this heart is not human, and it is the beginning of humaneness. 3A.5: the Mohist Yi Zhi reads the Documents' phrase 'as if protecting an infant' (若保赤子) as love without grades; Mencius replies that the phrase means something else: when an infant crawls towards a well, it is not the infant's fault.
rows.bearing: K1 (rule 9): Implied. Compassion is owed to any small child, not only one's own, but the passages describe a feeling, not a rule against killing. Reading 3A.5 as 'infants are without fault, so 7A.33 reaches them' is the researcher's inference; 7A.33 reaches newborns by its own plain words in any case.

rows.reference: Mencius 5B.4 (ctext Wan Zhang II, 4; Legge V.B.4; Kanripo inline 10.4), quoting the Announcement to Kang (Kang Gao) of the Classic of Documents
rows.original: 殺越人于貨，閔不畏死，凡民罔不譈 … 是不待教而誅者也
rows.translation: Chinese read in Kanripo KR1h0001 (TLS base text); Legge (1861; 1895) not displayed; paraphrase is the project's own
rows.says: Asked whether one may accept gifts from a man who robs travellers outside the city gate, Mencius says no, and quotes the Documents: those who kill people to seize their goods, reckless and unafraid of death, are hated by all the people. Such men are put to death without waiting to teach them; each dynasty received this law.
rows.bearing: K0 (gain): Clear teaching, through an approved quotation, that killing people for their goods is among the gravest wrongs. The execution of such killers is court context (rule 5), not a private licence to kill robbers. Now verified; it supports K0's gain clause.

rows.reference: Mencius 3B.5 (ctext Teng Wen Gong II, 5; Legge III.B.5; Kanripo inline 6.5)
rows.original: 有童子以黍肉餉，殺而奪之 … 為匹夫匹婦復讎也
rows.translation: Chinese read in Kanripo KR1h0001 (TLS base text); Legge (1861; 1895) not displayed; paraphrase is the project's own
rows.says: The chief of Ge robbed those bringing food to the fields and killed those who would not hand it over, among them a boy carrying millet and meat. King Tang attacked Ge because of that boy, and all said he did it not to enrich himself but to avenge ordinary men and women. His campaigns punished rulers and comforted their peoples (誅其君，弔其民), 'taking only the cruel' (取其殘而已矣). Mencius also quotes the Great Declaration, 'killing and attack were spread abroad' (殺伐用張), of King Wu's campaign against the cruel.
rows.bearing: K0 (gain) and K1 (children): Clear teaching, through an approved story, that killing even a child to take his food is a grave wrong. Tang's 'revenge' is a punitive war by a ruler (rule 5, exclusion (b)), not private revenge. K3: a rightful campaign is aimed at the ruler and 'the cruel' and spares the people; the quoted line on spreading killing concerns 'the cruel' (殘), not non-combatants. Now verified.

rows.reference: Mencius 5A.2 and 5A.3 (ctext Wan Zhang I, 2 and 3; Legge V.A.2 and V.A.3; Kanripo inline 9.2 and 9.3)
rows.original: 仁人之於弟也，不藏怒焉，不宿怨焉，親愛之而已矣
rows.translation: Chinese read in Kanripo KR1h0001 (TLS base text); Legge (1861; 1895) not displayed; paraphrase is the project's own
rows.says: Shun's father and his half-brother Xiang tried to kill him, burning the granary he was repairing and filling in the well he was digging (5A.2). Wan Zhang objects that Shun as ruler punished four great criminals, among them 'killing the San Miao' (殺三苗), yet gave Xiang, who spent his days plotting to kill him, a fief. Mencius answers that a humane man does not store up anger or nurse resentment against his brother; he simply loves him. Shun had officers govern the fief and collect its taxes, so that Xiang could not oppress its people (5A.3).
rows.bearing: K0 (revenge): Clear teaching, through the model ruler, that one takes no revenge even on someone who tried to kill you. Its stated reason concerns a brother, so on its own it reaches kin only. A ruler's leniency to kin is a grading of punishment (court and ruler context, rule 5), not a permission to kill. Now verified.

rows.reference: Doctrine of the Mean, ch. 10 (Zhu Xi's division; Legge ch. X; Zhong Yong chapter of the Book of Rites)
rows.original: 寬柔以教，不報無道，南方之強也，君子居之
rows.translation: James Legge (1861), not displayed; paraphrased
rows.says: Asked by Zilu about strength, Confucius contrasts the strength of the south (teaching with breadth and gentleness, not repaying unreasonable conduct), in which the noble person abides, with the strength of the north (sleeping on weapons and armour, dying without regret), in which the forceful abide; he then urges a strength that holds to harmony and the mean.
rows.bearing: K0 (revenge): Clear teaching that the noble person does not retaliate for wrongs done to him. It is general, not about killing, and does not mention a parent's killer. Zhu Xi's gloss was not seen; Zheng Xuan is reported to gloss the south's strength as gentleness. Not used to decide K0 even when verified, because the same Book of Rites contains revenge passages that are excluded (see the fairness notes).

rows.reference: Analects 12.21 (ctext Yan Yuan 21; Legge XII.21), 16.7 and 16.10 (ctext Ji Shi 7 and 10; Legge XVI.7 and XVI.10)
rows.original: 一朝之忿，忘其身，以及其親，非惑與 ; 血氣方剛，戒之在鬭 ; 忿思難，見得思義
rows.translation: Chinese read in Kanripo KR1h0004 (TLS base text); Legge (1861; 1893) not displayed; paraphrase is the project's own
rows.says: 12.21: asked by Fan Chi how to resolve delusion, Confucius says that to forget yourself in one morning's anger and bring harm on your parents is delusion. 16.7: the noble person guards against three things: lust in youth; fighting in the prime of life, when the blood is strong; acquisitiveness in old age. 16.10: when angry he thinks of the trouble that may follow; when he sees a chance of gain he thinks of what is right.
rows.bearing: K0 (anger and gain): Clear teaching as a wider rule (rule 7): restrain anger and fighting, and test every gain by rightness. None names killing, so each counts only as a wider rule that includes killing in anger or for gain. Now verified; they support K0 but are not needed to decide it.

rows.reference: Analects 12.10 (ctext Yan Yuan 10; Legge XII.10)
rows.original: 愛之欲其生，惡之欲其死。既欲其生，又欲其死，是惑也
rows.translation: Chinese read in Kanripo KR1h0004 (TLS base text); Legge (1861; 1893) not displayed; paraphrase is the project's own
rows.says: Asked by Zizhang how to resolve delusion, Confucius says: to want someone to live when you love them and to die when you hate them, and so to want both, is delusion.
rows.bearing: K0 (hatred): it treats even wishing death on someone one hates as confusion. Implied as to the act of killing. Does not decide.

rows.reference: Analects 13.19 (ctext Zi Lu 19; Legge XIII.19), with 15.6 (ctext Wei Ling Gong 6; Legge XV.5) and 12.5 (ctext Yan Yuan 5; Legge XII.5)
rows.original: 雖之夷狄，不可棄也 ; 雖蠻貊之邦，行矣 ; 四海之內，皆兄弟也
rows.translation: Chinese read in Kanripo KR1h0004 (TLS base text); Legge (1861; 1893) not displayed; paraphrase is the project's own
rows.says: 13.19: asked by Fan Chi about humaneness, Confucius says be respectful at home, careful at work and loyal to others; even among the Yi and Di these may not be set aside. 15.6: speech that is loyal and true and conduct that is earnest will carry you even among foreign peoples. 12.5: Sima Niu grieves that he alone has no brothers; Zixia tells him that within the four seas all are brothers.
rows.bearing: Against limiting moral duties to one's own people or community: the same conduct is owed among foreigners. Implied for K1 (rule 7 scope), since none mentions killing. No counted text found limits the protection of life to Chinese people or to Confucians.

rows.reference: Analects 14.21 (Kanripo inline 14.21; Legge XIV.22)
rows.original: 陳成子弒簡公。孔子沐浴而朝，告於哀公曰：「陳恆弒其君，請討之。」
rows.translation: Chinese read in Kanripo KR1h0004 (TLS base text); Legge (1861; 1893) not displayed; paraphrase is the project's own
rows.says: When Chen Heng murdered Duke Jian of Qi, Confucius bathed, went to court and asked Duke Ai of Lu to punish him. Told to report to the three chief families, he did so, and they refused. Each time he said that, having followed behind the great officers, he did not dare not to report it.
rows.bearing: Even for the murder of a ruler, Confucius does not act on his own authority but asks those with authority to act. Implied support for the private-authority part of K1, in ruler and war context (rule 5).

rows.reference: Mencius 3B.9 (ctext Teng Wen Gong II, 9; Legge III.B.9; Kanripo inline 6.9) and 7B.26 (ctext Jin Xin II, 26; Legge VII.B.26; Kanripo inline 14.26, though the file's source tag reads 7B27)
rows.original: 無父無君，是禽獸也 … 無父無君，是周公所膺也 … 能言距楊墨者，聖人之徒也 ; 歸，斯受之而已矣
rows.translation: Chinese read in Kanripo KR1h0001 (TLS base text); Legge (1861; 1895) not displayed; paraphrase is the project's own
rows.says: 3B.9: Mencius says Yang Zhu's 'for myself' denies the ruler and Mozi's 'love without distinction' denies the father, and 'to have no father and no ruler is to be a beast'. He recalls Yu taming the flood, the Duke of Zhou subduing the Yi and Di and driving off wild beasts, and Confucius writing the Spring and Autumn; quoting an ode on smiting the Rong and Di, he says 'no father and no ruler' is what the Duke of Zhou smote. His own task is to set minds right and stop false teachings: whoever can oppose Yang and Mo in words is a follower of the sages. 7B.26: those who leave Mozi turn to Yang, and those who leave Yang turn to the Confucians; when they come back, simply receive them; those who argue with them now are like men who chase a stray pig into its pen and then tie its legs.
rows.bearing: Heterodox teachers are to be answered by argument and those who return simply received: Implied support that K1's protection reaches 'heretics'. The harshest counted lines on heterodoxy are also here: Yang and Mo's teachings make men 'beasts' and are 'what the Duke of Zhou smote'. The smiting refers to the Duke of Zhou's wars on the Rong and Di (war context, rule 5), and Mencius's own response is words, not force, so the passage neither licenses nor approves killing a heretic (rule 4). Implied either way; does not decide.

K1.label: Taught (Explicit for every innocent person; Clear teaching that even the guilty may be put to death only by the judge)
K1.reason:
Deciding texts, all Tier 1 and read directly in Kanripo (rule 1):
- Mencius 7A.33: 'to kill one person who has done no wrong is against humaneness' (殺一無罪、非仁也). Explicit. It names no limit by status, sex, age or faith, so by its plain words it reaches newborns, wives, slaves and servants, strangers and unbelievers (rules 7 and 9).
- Mencius 2A.2: the sages would not 'kill one innocent person' (殺一不辜) even to gain the realm. Explicit.
- Mencius 2B.8: a man who has killed may be put to death, but only by the criminal judge (為士師，則可以殺之). Clear teaching (an analogy whose premise is stated as plainly true). This covers 'the wicked' that 7A.33 does not: a son, kinsman, master, crowd or zealot acting on his own authority may not kill even a killer. That is exactly K1's private-authority reach (rule 5).
Supporting, also direct: Analects 15.24 and 12.2 (do not impose on others what you do not want yourself) and Mencius 7B.31 (fill out the heart that does not wish to harm anyone), as wider rules (rule 7). The Great Learning ch. 10 and Doctrine of the Mean ch. 13 (primary, search-verified) give the same rule. The label no longer depends on reading the Golden Rule as a wider rule.

Counter-search of counted texts: a direct sweep of every Analects and Mencius passage containing 殺, 讎, 仇, 報, 怨 or 賊 found no counted text that permits, commands or approves a private killing of any class (rule 2). Mencius 7B.7 presupposes revenge without approving it (rule 4). Mencius 7A.35 and Analects 13.18 limit a son's part in enforcement, not the victim's protection, and 7A.35 treats the ruler's father's killing as a crime to be arrested (rule 5). Mencius 1B.8, 3B.5 and 1B.11 concern rulers and war; 1B.7, 6B.7 ('punish the unfilial'), 7A.12 and Analects 12.19 concern a ruler's punishment (rule 5). Mencius 3B.9's 'what the Duke of Zhou smote' refers to war, and Mencius answers heterodox teachers by argument (rule 4). Mencius 4B.24 reports a killing and blames it (rule 4). Analects 14.34 limits a duty to forgive and is not a permission; one search found no classical commentator reading it as allowing revenge. No counted text addresses self-defence; K1 does not need it.

Uncounted canon, reported beside the label (rule 1; corpus.md and decision 4): the Book of Rites, Qu Li I (unverified) and Tan Gong I (wording verified by search, in Confucius's own mouth), commands a son's revenge; the Gongyang, Ding 4 (verified by search), permits it for an unjust killing; the Rites of Zhou lets a registered avenger kill 'without guilt'; the Zuo, Yin 4, approves a father's arranging his son's killing; Ming and Qing law left some private killings unpunished. The counted Four Books never cite these and give the killing of a killer to the judge (2B.8).

Consistency with other traditions: the label turns on decision 4, not on the content of the wider canon. The Confucian texts that match Numbers 35:26 to 27 (a kinsman's private revenge) are in Tier 2 not treated as primary, whereas Numbers is Tier 1; so Judaism is Contradicted and Confucianism is not. The same holds for the other hard cases: the Confucian analogues of Phinehas (Zuo, Yin 4), of Abū Dāwūd 4361 (the Tang Code's graded penalty for killing a slave) and of Seneca, De Ira 1.15.2 (Zuo, Xuan 4, a reported, unapproved call to kill an infant) all lie outside the counted texts. If the project lead counted the whole Book of Rites, as two of its chapters already are, Tan Gong I would make K1 Contradicted in the same way as Numbers 35, and the Rites of Zhou's registered revenge would raise Unclear (rule 6).

Remaining risk: the classical commentaries on Mencius 7B.7 and 2B.8 (Zhao Qi, Zhu Xi) were not available and could not be found by search. If a classical commentator reads a counted passage as approving a son's revenge, the label could become Unclear (rule 6).

K0.label: Taught (Explicit for killing for gain; Clear teaching for killing in anger, hatred or revenge)
K0.reason:
K0 is narrower than K1, so the same deciding texts teach it; the clause-by-clause support is direct and specific (rule 1):
- Gain: Mencius 2A.2 (would not kill one innocent person to gain the realm; Explicit) and 7A.33 (Explicit for every innocent victim, whatever the motive); Mencius 5B.4 (those who kill people to seize their goods are hated by all; Clear teaching through an approved quotation) and 3B.5 (killing a boy to take his food is a grave wrong; Clear teaching through an approved story); Analects 16.10 (at a chance of gain, think of what is right; wider rule).
- Anger and hatred: 7A.33 covers every innocent victim; Analects 12.21 (one morning's anger that forgets oneself and one's parents is delusion) and 16.7 (in the prime of life guard against fighting) are Clear teaching as wider rules; Analects 12.10 (wishing death on someone one hates is confusion) is Implied; Mencius 1B.3 ranks sword-drawing anger low (Implied).
- Revenge: Mencius 2B.8 (only the criminal judge may put even a killer to death, so a son may not kill his father's killer; Clear teaching); Mencius 5A.3 (the humane man stores no anger and nurses no resentment against a brother who tried to kill him; Clear teaching, reaching kin); Mencius 4B.28 (outrage is met by self-examination, not contention; Clear teaching as a wider rule for wrongs to oneself).
The Doctrine of the Mean ch. 10 (the noble person 'does not repay unreasonable conduct') is now search-verified but is still deliberately not used, because other chapters of the same Book of Rites that approve revenge are excluded.

Counter-evidence in counted texts: Mencius 7B.7 presupposes revenge without approving it (rule 4); Analects 14.34 ('repay injury with straightness') limits a duty to forgive and is not a permission; Mencius 2A.2's Beigong You, who returned every insult, is described, not approved, and set below a courage grounded in looking within (rule 4). None approves a killing for gain, anger, hatred or revenge.

The revenge clause is exactly where the uncounted canon differs: the Book of Rites commands revenge (Qu Li I unverified; Tan Gong I wording verified by search), the Gongyang (Ding 4) and the Rites of Zhou allow a son's revenge for a parent killed unjustly, and Liu Zongyuan defends it. Counted, they would make K0 Contradicted (Book of Rites) or at least Unclear (Rites of Zhou). The same dependency on decision 4 and the same unchecked commentary on Mencius 7B.7 apply as for K1.

K3.label: Taught (Clear teaching); 'those who have surrendered' is not named in a counted text
K3.reason:
Deciding texts, all Tier 1 and read directly in Kanripo (rule 1):
- Mencius 1B.11: after Qi takes Yan, Mencius asks how it can be right to kill the people's fathers and elder brothers and carry off their sons and younger brothers, and tells the king to send back the old and the young (反其旄倪). Clear teaching that a conquering army must not kill or seize the conquered people, with the old and young named.
- Mencius 7B.4: King Wu tells the people of Yin, 'I am not the enemy of the people' (非敵百姓也); boasting of skill in battle is a great crime.
- Mencius 3B.5: Tang's campaigns 'punished the rulers and comforted the people' and took 'only the cruel'.
- Mencius 7B.3: Mencius refuses to believe a record of blood flowing enough to float pestles, because the most humane would not slaughter.
- Supporting: 1A.6 (only one who does not delight in killing can unite the realm), 4A.14 (those good at war deserve the heaviest punishment), 6B.8 (a humane man would not seek land by killing people).
They teach through counsel to kings and approved stories, so Clear teaching, not Explicit.

Limits and counter-evidence: Mencius accepts punitive war by a humane ruler (1B.8, 3B.5; 2B.8 reserves it to a 'minister of Heaven'), and 3B.5 quotes 'killing and attack were spread abroad' (殺伐用張) approvingly, but of war against 'the cruel', not non-combatants. No counted text names those who have surrendered: 7B.4's people bowing their heads to the ground and 4B.24's archer sparing an enemy too sick to hold his bow (Implied; the motive is loyalty to a line of teachers) are the nearest. No counted text approves killing non-combatants.

Uncounted context: the Documents' battle oaths threaten disobedient soldiers with punishment together with their children (verified by search); the Zuo and Gongyang disagree on sparing the wounded and the grey-haired (unverified); the Book of Rites has Confucius praise an archer's restraint (unverified).

The label no longer rests on the Golden Rule as a wider rule, so it is no longer borderline. K3 is a record wording, not part of the floor.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: Mencius 2A.2 is listed as a deciding Explicit text, but it is ruler context. Read directly (KR1h0001_003.txt, MENG 2A02:27): 得百里之地而君之 ... 殺一不辜，而得天下，皆不為也. The sages are imagined as rulers of a hundred li, and the killing in view is one done to gain the realm, which is the kind of killing a ruler orders. Rule 5 says such texts are context only and never decide a label, in either direction. It is good a fortiori support (if a sage would not kill one innocent person even for the realm, a private person may not kill for less), but it should not be counted as deciding. The same applies to its use as 'Explicit' for K0's gain clause.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 5 (exclusion (a), a ruler's order; texts on rulers are context only); rule 1 (which texts decide).
objections.proposed: List only Mencius 7A.33 (addressed to a 士, a private person: KR1h0001_013.txt, MENG 7A33:01 to 02) and 2B.8 as deciding texts for K1 and K0. Move 2A.2 to supporting, marked 'ruler context; a fortiori support'. No label change, because 7A.33 alone is Explicit for every innocent victim whatever the motive.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: 7A.33 protects only those 'without guilt' (無罪), and the counted texts themselves make some classes guilty and punishable: Mencius 6B.7 gives 'punish the unfilial' (誅不孝) as the first command of a covenant Mencius holds up as a standard, and 5B.4 approves executing robber-killers 'without waiting to teach them'. So 7A.33 does not reach a disobedient child, an offending slave or servant, an adulterous wife or 'the wicked' generally. For all of them, and for a kinsman's killer, K1 rests on Mencius 2B.8 alone. And 2B.8 names only a killer (殺人者). Its exclusivity is implied, not stated: 為士師，則可以殺之 means 'if he is the criminal judge, he may kill him'. The word 'only' is not in the text. The proposed label presents the reach to the guilty as if it were as firm as 7A.33. It is one analogy inside an argument about war. If 2B.8 were read as Implied, K1 would fall to 'Taught in part' (innocent persons only).
objections.rule_basis: Rule 7 (the counted text must reach everyone K1 protects, including 'the wicked'; a duty owed to only some people is 'taught in part'); METHOD.md section 3 (Clear teaching must not be stretched).
objections.proposed: Keep 2B.8 at Clear teaching, but state why. (1) Mencius's argument works only if the authority is exclusive: if anyone might kill a killer, anyone might attack Yan, and his reply 以燕伐燕 would fail. (2) He applies the same principle to states (天吏), which shows that it is a general rule about authority to punish, not a rule special to killers. (3) Read directly: Mencius 6B.7 gives the same principle (天子討而不伐; 無專殺大夫), and 7A.35 calls Gao Yao 士 and makes the judge's arrest the right response even when the killer is the ruler's own father (瞽瞍殺人 ... 執之而已矣). State in the label that the reach to the guilty rests on 2B.8 read as a general rule of authority, supported by 6B.7 and 7A.35, and that without it K1 would be 'Taught in part'.

objections.label: K0
objections.objection: The counted texts never condemn revenge as a motive. Read directly: Mencius 3B.5:05 approves Tang's war because 'all within the four seas' called it 'revenge for ordinary men and women' (為匹夫匹婦復讎也). 7B.7 presupposes a son's revenge without blaming it. Analects 14.34 refuses a duty to repay injury with kindness. What they teach against revenge is narrower: restraint of resentment for wrongs to oneself (4B.28), restraint toward a brother who tried to kill oneself (5A.3), and the rule that only the judge may kill a killer (2B.8). So the case the uncounted canon actually commands, avenging a parent or brother, rests on 2B.8 alone. Also, 5A.3's setting is a ruler's treatment of his brother (Wan Zhang contrasts Shun's punishments as Son of Heaven with his enfeoffing Xiang), so only its stated maxim counts as a personal rule (仁人之於弟也，不藏怒焉，不宿怨焉). Missed counter row, read directly in a sweep for 誅: Mencius 1B.12 approves Zengzi's 'what goes out from you comes back to you' (出乎爾者，反乎爾者也) when the people of Zou let their officers die in battle unaided. That is a tit-for-tat principle about deaths, but it involves no killing and is in war context, so it is Implied (rule 4) and does not decide.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 4 (presupposing and reporting are not approving); rule 5 (3B.5 and 1B.12 are war and ruler context); METHOD.md section 3 rule 3 (no cherry-picking: show passages on both sides).
objections.proposed: Restate the revenge clause: 'Clear teaching for revenge for wrongs to oneself or by kin against oneself (4B.28; 5A.3's maxim; supporting Analects 5.23, Bo Yi and Shu Qi 不念舊惡). Avenging a parent or brother is excluded only by the authority rule of 2B.8, not by any counted condemnation of revenge as a motive.' Add 3B.5 (revenge as an approved war aim) and 1B.12 as counter or context rows (Implied, do not decide).

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: The label line itself reads as unconditional, but K1 and K0 depend entirely on decision 4. The rows themselves say that every historical branch, Cheng-Zhu included, held the Book of Rites as a classic, and the project already counts two of its chapters (the Great Learning and the Doctrine of the Mean) as primary. Tan Gong I, whose wording is verified by search, puts a command of private revenge in Confucius's own mouth. Under the brief's rule 1 ('NOT the Five Classics') the label is correct. But a reader comparing it with Judaism (Numbers 35:26 to 27, Contradicted) needs to see in the label, not only in the reasons, that the difference comes from the corpus line and not from the content. A branch question is also unexamined. Decision 3 treats Han to Tang classical learning as a historical school. Whether any living Confucian body today holds the Five Classics or the Gongyang as scripture (a lead from general knowledge, not checked and not evidence, for example modern Confucian religious organisations and the modern Gongyang revival) has not been examined. If one met decision 3's test, rule 3 would give 'Contradicted in one branch': Tan Gong I or Gongyang Ding 4, both of which permit or command a son's revenge, once Tan Gong I's placement is verified. The same applies to K0.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 1 and rule 3 (counting and branches); METHOD.md section 9, decisions 3 and 4.
objections.proposed: Add to the K1 and K0 label lines: 'conditional on decision 4 (the Book of Rites not counted); if it were counted, Contradicted (Tan Gong I, once its placement is verified)'. Record for the project lead the open question of whether any living Confucian body that holds the Five Classics as scripture is a branch under decision 3. No label change unless that is checked and confirmed.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: Rule 6 makes a classical commentator's narrowing reading decisive for Unclear, and corpus.md names Zhao Qi and Zhu Xi as the standard commentaries for reconciliation. Neither was read on the deciding text 2B.8, on 7B.7 or on Analects 14.34; the 14.34 lead was searched only once, through a summary. The proposal drops the earlier 'provisional' marker while these checks remain open. None of the reconciliation rows shows any Confucian authority citing 2B.8 against revenge, so its reach to a son's revenge is so far the project's own reading. That is plain on the words, but untested against the tradition's reading.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 6 (classical commentators); corpus.md section 6 (standard commentaries); METHOD.md section 3 rule 3 (reconciliation from the tradition's own authorities).
objections.proposed: Label K1 and K0 'Taught (provisional)' until Zhao Qi and Zhu Xi on Mencius 2B.8 and 7B.7, and the classical readings of 直 in Analects 14.34, are read. Name these as the next research step.

objections.label: K3
objections.objection: The strongest case for too gentle: the wording names four classes, the label itself says one of them ('those who have surrendered') is not named in a counted text, and rule 7 makes a duty that reaches only some protected people 'taught in part'. The strongest case against: read directly (MENG 1B11:04), 1B.11 concerns a population that had welcomed the army with food and drink (簞食壺漿以迎王師), so it had submitted. Mencius condemns killing its adult men (若殺其父兄 ... 如之何其可也) without asking whether they had borne arms. In 7B.4 the people bow to the ground (稽首) and are told 'I am not the enemy of the people'. These reach people who have given up resistance, which is what 'those who have surrendered' picks out, even though no text deals with soldiers laying down arms in battle. Also, 1B.11's argument is partly prudential (是動天下之兵也, 'this will set the armies of the realm moving'). The moral question comes first, so Clear teaching stands, but the prudential half should be recorded.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 7 ('taught in part'); METHOD.md section 3 (Clear teaching not to be stretched).
objections.proposed: Keep 'Taught (Clear teaching)'. Replace the note with: 'those who have surrendered are reached in substance through a conquered population that had submitted (1B.11, 7B.4); no counted text deals with fighters who lay down arms in battle (4B.24 is Implied)'. Record 1B.11's prudential second argument.

objections.label: K3
objections.objection: A counter row is missing. Read directly (KR1h0001_006.txt, MENG 3B09:05): the Duke of Zhou 'drove Fei Lian to the edge of the sea and killed him' (驅飛廉於海隅而戮之) and 'destroyed fifty states' (滅國者五十), and 'the realm rejoiced' (天下大悅). Mencius tells this with approval. Fei Lian was a minister of the tyrant who was fleeing, and the text does not show him fighting. 滅國 means extinguishing states as polities, and the text does not say that people who were not fighting were killed. So it is Implied for K3, and the Fei Lian killing is closer to a ruler's punishment of a tyrant's servant (rule 5) than to killing a civilian. But it is the counted text's own approval of war's destruction and should be shown next to 1B.11 and 7B.3.
objections.rule_basis: METHOD.md section 3 rules 2 and 3 (search for counter-evidence; show both sides); rule 4 (approval must reach the act the wording forbids).
objections.proposed: Add Mencius 3B.9:05 as a K3 counter row: 'approved destruction of fifty states and killing of a fleeing enemy minister; non-combatants not named; Implied; does not decide'. No label change.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: Mencius 7A.35 is understated as merely 'limiting a son's part in enforcement'. Mencius approves Shun carrying his father, a killer, beyond the law's reach for life (竊負而逃，遵海濱而處，終身訢然). An adherent of the victim's family would notice that the approved outcome is a killing left unpunished. It is still not permission to kill: Gao Yao's arrest is right and Shun cannot forbid it. It is also not graded protection under rule 2, which concerns who the victim is or what the victim did, not who the killer's son is.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 2 (what counts as permission or graded protection); rule 5 (court context).
objections.proposed: Reword the row: 'Mencius approves a son removing his killer father from punishment; the killing itself remains a crime that the judge must arrest; no permission to kill and no graded protection of any class of victim; does not decide.'

objections.label: K0
objections.objection: The direct sweep missed some supporting and weak counter passages. I read them directly. Supporting: Analects 11.24 (even retainers of the Ji house 'would not follow in killing a father or ruler', 弒父與君，亦不從也: a refusal to join a killing ordered by a household head); Analects 5.23 (Bo Yi and Shu Qi did not remember old wrongs, 不念舊惡); Mencius 4B.30 ('fondness for courage and fighting that endangers one's parents' is among the five things 'the world calls unfilial', a common view that Mencius uses without dissent, so Implied). Weak counter: Analects 5.25 (Confucius finds it shameful to hide resentment and befriend the person, 匿怨而友其人; this accepts open resentment but says nothing of harm, so Implied). Separately, the project uses Doctrine of the Mean ch. 13 and Great Learning ch. 10 as counted support but sets aside Doctrine of the Mean ch. 10 because other Book of Rites chapters are excluded. Under decision 4 the two Four Books chapters are either counted or not. They cannot be counted for one passage and set aside for another.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 1 (counted texts); METHOD.md section 3 rules 2 and 3.
objections.proposed: Add Analects 11.24 and 5.23 as supporting rows (Clear teaching as wider rules for K0's revenge clause and for refusing a household head's order to kill), and Mencius 4B.30 and Analects 5.25 as Implied. Treat Doctrine of the Mean ch. 10 as counted support like ch. 13 (VERIFIED (search) only, so it could not be counted in an admitted article under decision 6). No label change.

K1.label: Taught (provisional; conditional on decision 4). Explicit for every innocent person (Mencius 7A.33). Clear teaching (Mencius 2B.8, supported by 6B.7 and 7A.35) that only the judge may put anyone to death, which alone carries the guilty and a kinsman's killer.
K1.reason: 7A.33 (read directly) is addressed to a 士, a private person, and names no limit by status, sex, age or faith. So it reaches every innocent person, newborns included (rules 7 and 9). It does not reach the guilty, and the counted texts make some classes guilty (6B.7 誅不孝; 5B.4). For them, and for the killer of one's kin, the only deciding text is 2B.8: asked who may kill a killer, Mencius answers 'the criminal judge'. The exclusivity is carried by the argument, since otherwise 以燕伐燕 fails, and is generalised by Mencius himself to states (天吏). Read directly, 6B.7 (天子討而不伐; 無專殺大夫) and 7A.35 (the judge 士 arrests even the ruler's father) state the same principle. That is enough for Clear teaching, but if 2B.8 were judged Implied, K1 would be 'Taught in part'. 2A.2 is ruler context (rule 5), so it is a fortiori support, not deciding. No counted text permits, commands or approves a private killing of any class. 7B.7 only presupposes revenge (rule 4); 7A.35 approves a son removing his killer father from punishment but treats the killing as a crime (not rule 2); 3B.9 answers heretics with words. Provisional because Zhao Qi and Zhu Xi on 2B.8 and 7B.7, and classical readings of 直 in Analects 14.34, are unchecked (rule 6). Conditional because the Book of Rites, held as a classic by every historical branch, commands a son's revenge (Tan Gong I, wording verified by search, placement not). If it were counted, or if a living body holding the Five Classics or the Gongyang as scripture were found to be a branch under decision 3 (an unchecked lead), the result would be Contradicted, or Contradicted in one branch.

K0.label: Taught (provisional; conditional on decision 4). Explicit where the victim is innocent, whatever the motive (7A.33). Clear teaching for gain (5B.4, 3B.5), anger (Analects 12.21, 16.7 as wider rules) and revenge for wrongs to oneself or by kin (4B.28; 5A.3's maxim). Avenging a parent or brother is excluded only by 2B.8's authority rule.
K0.reason: K0 is narrower than K1, so the K1 texts carry it. 7A.33 is Explicit for any motive where the victim is innocent. The gain clause has 5B.4 (killing travellers for goods is hated by all, an approved quotation) and 3B.5 (killing a boy for his food). 2A.2 is ruler context and only supports. The anger clause has Analects 12.21 and 16.7 as wider rules, with 12.10 and Mencius 1B.3 Implied. The revenge clause is the weak point. The counted texts do not condemn revenge as a motive: 3B.5 approves Tang's war as 'revenge for ordinary men and women' (war context), 7B.7 presupposes a son's revenge, and Analects 14.34 refuses a duty to return kindness for injury. They teach restraint for wrongs to oneself (4B.28; Analects 5.23 supporting) and toward a brother (5A.3's personal maxim; its ruler setting is context). For the killer of a parent or brother they rely on 2B.8 alone, which is Clear teaching on the reasoning given for K1. Mencius 1B.12 (an approved tit-for-tat maxim about officers left to die) involves no killing and is war context, so it is Implied. The same provisional status (unchecked commentary on 2B.8, 7B.7 and 14.34) and the same dependence on decision 4 apply. Counted, the Book of Rites (Tan Gong I) or the Gongyang (Ding 4) would make the revenge clause Contradicted, and the Rites of Zhou's registered avenger would make it Unclear.

K3.label: Taught (Clear teaching). Those who have surrendered are reached in substance through a conquered population that had submitted (1B.11, 7B.4); no counted text deals with fighters who lay down arms in battle.
K3.reason: Read directly. Mencius 1B.11: Yan's people had welcomed Qi's army with food and drink, and Mencius asks how killing their fathers and elder brothers and binding their sons could be right, then tells the king to send back the old and the young. That is Clear teaching that a conquering army must not kill a population that has stopped resisting, adult men included. The text adds a prudential argument, which should be recorded. 7B.4: King Wu tells the people of Yin, who bow to the ground, 'I am not the enemy of the people', and boasting of skill in battle is a great crime. 3B.5: a rightful campaign punishes the ruler, comforts the people and takes 'only the cruel'. 7B.3: Mencius rejects a record of blood floating pestles, because the most humane would not slaughter. Supporting: 1A.6, 4A.14, 6B.8. Counter or context: 3B.5's approved 殺伐用張 concerns 'the cruel'. 3B.9:05 (missing from the rows) approves the Duke of Zhou destroying fifty states and killing the fleeing minister Fei Lian. Non-combatants are not named there, and the Fei Lian killing is closer to a ruler's punishment, so it is Implied and does not decide. 4B.24's archer is Implied. Uncounted texts (the Documents' 孥戮 oaths, Zuo and Gongyang on the Hong river, Tan Gong II's archer) are reported beside the label. K3 is a record wording, not part of the floor.

challenge.consistency_notes: The proposed treatment matches the other traditions on the one point that drives the result: only counted texts decide (rule 1), and the Five Classics are not counted (decision 4). This is the same footing as the Mahabharata for Hinduism and the Pahlavi books for Zoroastrianism. Hard case by hard case. Numbers 35:26 to 27 (a kinsman kills a court-judged manslayer, 'no bloodguilt') is Tier 1 for Judaism and Christianity, so Contradicted. Its Confucian analogues are Tan Gong I and Qu Li I (a son's revenge commanded), Gongyang Ding 4 (permitted for an unjust killing) and the Rites of Zhou's registered avenger (Unclear, judicial or private). All are uncounted, so they are reported, not deciding. The difference comes from the corpus line, not the content, and the label line should say so. Phinehas: the analogue is Zuo Yin 4 (大義滅親). It is uncounted and unverified, and its judicial or private character is disputed, so it would be Unclear if counted. Abū Dāwūd 4361 (Sunni-graded under decision 5, so counted for Sunni Islam): the analogues are the Guliang's death for mocking a ruler (carried out by an officer, so ruler context, and uncounted) and the Ming and Qing exemptions for killing an adulterer or a parent's killer on the spot (state law outside the corpus). If any counted Confucian text declared such a killing unpunished, it would be Contradicted on the same footing. Seneca, De Ira 1.15.2 (a Tier 1 approval of drowning newborns): the analogues are Zuo Xuan 4 (uncounted, and a report of counsel the father refused, so Implied under rule 4 even if counted) and Guo Ju (outside the corpus, rejected by the Ming ruling). No counted Confucian text approves killing an infant. Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra (a branch-specific counted text, so Contradicted in one branch): no branch-specific counted Confucian text was found. But whether any living Confucian body holding the Five Classics or the Gongyang as scripture counts as a branch under decision 3 has not been examined, and it is the one route by which rule 3 could apply. Yasna 31.18 and 33.2 (resisting the follower of the Lie): the nearest counted analogue is Mencius 3B.9, where heterodoxy is 'what the Duke of Zhou smote', but Mencius specifies a response in words (能言距楊墨者) and 7B.26 says to receive those who return. So it is Implied and does not decide, which is consistent provided the Zoroastrian label turned on a text that names weapons or harm. Atharvaveda rites and Bṛhadāraṇyaka 6.4.12 (Tier 1 ritual killing of enemies or a wife's lover): there is no Confucian counted analogue. The Book of Rites' execution of diviners and deviant teachers (Wang Zhi) is a ruler's law, so rule 5 context, and is uncounted. One internal consistency point: the Great Learning and Doctrine of the Mean are counted Book of Rites chapters, so Doctrine of the Mean ch. 10 should be treated as counted support like ch. 13 rather than set aside. Neither decides. Labels whose reach depends on one analogy (2B.8) should carry that dependence in the label, as the other traditions' labels carry theirs.
